Prepare actual greetings and protocol examples

Adult uses a school-approved local First Nations language source or local language centre to confirm a greeting, its language, meaning, pronunciation model and appropriate use. Read or hear that actual model with the child; compare with another verified greeting from a family or community source. Record the sources; do not invent a local word or assume a language from a map boundary. A Welcome to Country is delivered by Traditional Owners or Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander people with their permission. Anyone can offer an Acknowledgement of Country respectfully. Compare these purposes and roles using an authorised actual example. This is observation and discussion, not a classroom imitation of a Welcome or ceremony.

Improve card 4 using an actual supplied detail or a detail from an actual book you have read. Six complete original samples for comparison

Actual connected texts for reference and omission

Repetitive draft: “Mia found Mia’s hat. Mia put Mia’s hat on. The hat was Mia’s.” Clear version: “Mia found her hat. She put it on. The hat was hers.” Her, She and hers refer to Mia; it refers to the hat. Alex says: “I chose red paint. Sam chose blue.” The omitted word after blue is paint. Dialogue: “Who watered the seeds?” “Jo did.” The reply means Jo watered the seeds. Ambiguous draft: “Mia met Ava. She carried the bag.” Either person could be She; name the intended person to repair it. Association chain: “Isy is a student. Her sister calls her Isy. Isy says, ‘I enjoy reading.’” Track Isy/her/I without assuming that every related noun means the same person.

Actual word cards and sentences

Cards: articles a / an / the; adjectives small / brown / tall / noisy; nouns dog / tree / parrots. Build meaningful groups such as “the small brown dog” and “a tall tree”. Plain sentences: “The dog barked.” “A bird flew.” Add an accurate useful noun detail, then compare a suitable verb group: “The small dog was barking.” “The noisy bird is flying.” In “The small dog was barking”, the whole noun group is The small dog and the whole verb group is was barking. In “The ball was touched”, was touched is the verb group. Compare “two pairs of old walking shoes”: the extra words specify quantity, condition and type. Use familiar examples; longer is not automatically better.

Actual vocabulary contexts and revision paragraph

Garden topic: “Water goes through the long tube to the plants.” A garden hose is a flexible tube for carrying water; hose is a precise choice for this context. Story topic: “The character spoke very quietly so the sleeping baby would not wake.” Whispered fits that stated meaning; shouted would change it. Draft: “The person went to the quiet garden. The person said something softly. The place was nice.” One possible new fictional version: “The gardener walked to the peaceful garden. The gardener whispered.” This deliberately adds an occupation and new action details; it is a changed story, not a fact-preserving edit of the draft. For an edit that keeps the original facts, do not add those details. In a fictional story, magician, wizard and sorcerer can describe different imagined characters; use the actual author’s clues rather than assume the nouns always mean exactly the same thing. Timid describes a shy or hesitant response; frightened names fear. Choose the word that fits the actual action clues.

Actual title and list editing cards

For this activity, use title case: capitalise the first word and main words; keep internal a, an, the, and, or, to and of lower-case unless part of a proper name. Title cards: “the red kite”; “a walk to the pond”; “mia and the moon”. Models: “The Red Kite”, “A Walk to the Pond”, “Mia and the Moon”. Another valid style is sentence case: “A walk to the pond”. Apply the declared style for the task. List draft: “We packed a red hat two blue pens a ruler and paper.” Whole items: a red hat / two blue pens / a ruler / paper. Edit: “We packed a red hat, two blue pens, a ruler and paper.” A clear serial comma before and is also accepted unless a stated style excludes it. Do not split red from hat or blue from pens. End the sentence with its full stop.
